Guided Inquiry

1 · The apparatus

A horizontal pipe carries water left to right. It is wide at the ends and narrow in the middle (the throat). Two open vertical tubes — manometers — stand on the pipe: one on the wide inlet, one on the throat. The fluid rises inside each tube to a height that reads out the pressure at that station.

Right now the throat is as wide as the inlet, so nothing is being squeezed. Press ▶ Play and watch the flow. Then continue.

2 · Predict — narrow the throat

You are about to shrink the throat with the Throat area slider. What happens to the fluid level in the throat manometer, compared to the inlet manometer?

3 · Observe

Drag the Throat area slider down. Watch two things at once:

• the particles crowd and speed up through the throat — that is continuity, A₁v₁ = A₂v₂;
• the throat manometer column falls below the inlet one — that is Bernoulli, faster fluid = lower pressure.

The height difference Δh between the two columns IS the pressure drop: ΔP = ρ g Δh. Read it on the right.

4 · The one thing to notice

Squeezing the pipe does not push the fluid harder — it makes the fluid faster, and a faster fluid pushes sideways LESS.

The squeeze goes into speed, not into pressure. That is why the throat manometer falls, and that is the whole Venturi effect — the reason carburettors, atomisers and airspeed indicators work.

The Physics

The Venturi — A Narrowing Pipe · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

Water flows through a horizontal pipe that narrows to a throat. Two open tubes stand on the pipe, one at the wide inlet and one at the throat, and the water level in each tube shows the pressure there.

What you'll learn

  • How the speed of the water at the throat depends on the throat area.
  • How the pressure at the throat compares with the pressure at the inlet.
  • How the gap between the two water levels depends on the throat area and on the inlet speed.
Wide inlet (A1), narrow throat (A2), and one open tube on each.

What's on screen

  • Pipe and moving water: blue dots carry the flow from left to right.
  • Two tubes (pink): the water level in each one shows the pressure at its station.
  • Δh bracket (teal): the gap between the two water levels, with its value in metres.
  • Readouts (sidebar): Throat speed v₂ and Manometer Δh.
See itOpen the sim with its opening values: A₂ = 0.0100 m² and v₁ = 2.00 m/s. Watch for: a straight pipe with the dots moving right, the labels A₁ and A₂, and both tubes at the same level.

Fixed: the inlet area A₁ = 0.0100 m², the fluid is water with ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s², and the inlet pressure is P₁ = 101 325 Pa.

03

A narrower pipe makes the water faster

Water is nearly incompressible, so in steady flow the same volume must pass every station each second. This volume flow rate is Q = A v, and it has the same value at the inlet and at the throat.

A1 v1 = A2 v2  ⟹  v2 = (A1 / A2) v1
Continuity: mass conservation for steady flow of an incompressible fluid.

At the opening v1 = 2.00 m/s, Q = 0.0100 × 2.00 = 0.0200 m³/s. Halve the throat to A2 = 0.0050 m² and the same Q needs v2 = 0.0200 / 0.0050 = 4.00 m/s. The narrowest throat, 0.0020 m², gives 10.00 m/s.

See itKeep v₁ = 2.00 and set A₂ = 0.0050 m². Watch for: Throat speed v₂ reading 4.00 m/s and the dots crowding together and moving faster through the narrow part.
04

Faster water has lower pressure

Bernoulli's equation says that along a horizontal streamline in a steady, frictionless flow, P + ½ρv² has the same value at every point.

P1 + ½ρv1² = P2 + ½ρv2²  ⟹  ΔP = P1 − P2 = ½ρ(v2² − v1²)
Station 1 is the inlet and station 2 is the throat.

Where v is larger, ½ρv² is larger, so P must be smaller. Squeezing the pipe does not push the water harder. The water speeds up, and some of its pressure is spent on that extra speed. With A₂ = 0.0050 m² and v₁ = 2.00 m/s, v₂ = 4.00 m/s, so ΔP = ½ × 1000 × (16 − 4) = 6000 Pa. The throat pressure is 95 325 Pa, against 101 325 Pa at the inlet.

See itKeep v₁ = 2.00 and set A₂ = 0.0050 m². Watch for: the throat tube standing lower than the inlet tube, with a bracket labelled Δh = 0.612 m between them.
05

The gap between the water levels measures the pressure drop

A column of water of height h exerts pressure ρgh. The gap Δh between the two levels is therefore the pressure drop ΔP written as a height of water:

Δh = ΔP / (ρg) = (v2² − v1²) / 2g
The tubes hold the same fluid as the pipe, so ρ cancels and Δh does not depend on it.
A₂ (m²), v₁ = 2.00v₂ (m/s)ΔP (Pa)Δh (m)
0.01002.0000.000

0.00258.0030 0003.058
0.002010.0048 0004.893

The sim draws the inlet column at a fixed height on screen. Only the gap between the two columns is to scale.

See itKeep v₁ = 2.00 and narrow the throat to A₂ = 0.0020 m². Watch for: the throat tube far below the inlet tube, with Δh = 4.893 m and Throat speed 10.00 m/s.
06

Doubling the inlet speed quadruples the gap

For a fixed throat, v2 = (A1/A2) v1 is proportional to v1. Then v2² − v1² is proportional to v1², and so is Δh.

With A₂ = 0.0050 m², where v₂ = 2v₁, Δh = 3v₁² / 2g:

v₁ (m/s)v₂ (m/s)Δh (m)
1.002.000.153
2.004.000.612
4.008.002.446

Both the narrowing and the speed matter. At v₁ = 0.50 m/s and A₂ = 0.0020 m², Δh is 0.306 m. At v₁ = 4.00 m/s and A₂ = 0.0075 m² it is 0.634 m, from a much gentler narrowing.

Go deeper: where the sim goes beyond a real pipe

The sim never limits Δh. At A₂ = 0.0020 m² and v₁ above about 2.9 m/s, ΔP exceeds the fixed P₁ = 101 325 Pa, so the formula gives a negative absolute pressure at the throat. Real water cannot do that. It would form vapour bubbles first, an effect called cavitation.

See itSet A₂ = 0.0050 m² and push v₁ to 4.00 m/s. Watch for: Throat speed 8.00 m/s and the gap growing to Δh = 2.446 m, four times the 0.612 m at v₁ = 2.00.
07

Where it matters

  • Venturi meters. They measure the pressure drop between a wide section and a throat. Inverting the formulas gives v1, and so the flow rate Q, without touching the flow.
  • Carburettors and sprayers. Air speeds up in a narrow part of the tube, its pressure falls, and the higher outside pressure pushes fuel or liquid into the stream.
  • Filter pumps. A fast jet of water through a narrow nozzle lowers the pressure beside it. The lab pump uses this to draw air out of a flask.
  • Airspeed indicators. Aircraft compare the pressure of the oncoming air with the surrounding pressure. The difference ½ρv² gives the speed.
08

Summary

In one line. This sim narrows a pipe and shows how the speed of the water and the pressure in it are linked through two tubes.

Key points

  • Continuity: A1 v1 = A2 v2, so a smaller area gives a larger speed.
  • Bernoulli: P + ½ρv² is constant along a horizontal streamline, so a larger speed gives a lower pressure.
  • The gap between the two water levels is Δh = (v2² − v1²) / 2g.

Common mix-ups

  • "A narrow pipe squeezes the water, so the pressure there is higher." The squeeze raises the speed. At the same height the pressure there is lower.
  • "The water speeds up because the pipe pushes it." The speed follows from conservation of the volume flow rate Q, not from a push.
  • "Δh depends on the fluid's density." In ΔP = ρgΔh the ρ cancels with the ρ in ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²).

Things to try on your own

  • Predict v₂ and Δh for A₂ = 0.0040 m² with v₁ = 2.00 m/s, then check them in the sim.
  • Set v₁ = 0.50 m/s and narrow the throat as far as it goes. Compare the gap with the one at v₁ = 4.00.
  • Find an A₂ and v₁ for which Δh is about 1 m.
